5.5.paragraph: The twinkling of stars, known to astronomers as scintillation, originates not in the stars but in Earth's turbulent atmosphere. shared.title: The Green Revolution in Agriculture
shared.text:
In the middle of the twentieth century, many experts feared that the world's rapidly growing population would soon outstrip its food supply. Yet over the following decades, grain production in many developing countries rose dramatically. This transformation, known as the Green Revolution, was driven largely by new crop varieties and modern farming methods.

At the center of these changes was the American plant scientist Norman Borlaug, who began developing high-yielding varieties of wheat in Mexico in the 1940s. His wheat plants had short, sturdy stems. Traditional tall varieties often fell over when heavy heads of grain formed, especially when farmers applied fertilizer, but the shorter plants could support much larger harvests. Similar high-yielding rice varieties were later developed in the Philippines. In the late 1960s, India and Pakistan adopted the new wheat and saw their harvests increase rapidly. Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 for his work.

However, the Green Revolution also had costs. The new crops needed large amounts of fertilizer, pesticides, and irrigation water, which polluted rivers and depleted groundwater in some regions. In addition, wealthier farmers, who could afford these inputs, often benefited more than poorer ones. For these reasons, many researchers today are looking for ways to raise yields while using fewer resources.

lines.text: Hi, I have an appointment at two. My sociology professor said my essay is hard to follow, and I'm not sure how to fix it.

lines.text: I see. That's actually a really common problem. When you organize by source, the reader has to figure out your argument on their own. It works better to organize by idea.

shared.title: The placebo effect
shared.text:
Okay, today we're looking at one of the strangest findings in medicine: the placebo effect. A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, like a sugar pill or an injection of salt water. You'd expect it to do nothing. But in study after study, a lot of patients who get a placebo report that they feel better.

So why does that happen? A big part of it is expectation. When patients believe a treatment will help, the brain can actually change how the body responds. Pain is the clearest example. When people expect a pill to relieve pain, the brain can release its own natural painkillers, called endorphins. And here's the interesting part: when researchers give patients a drug that blocks endorphins, much of that placebo pain relief goes away. So it isn't just imagination. Something physical is going on.

The setting matters, too. A confident doctor, a professional-looking clinic, even the color and size of a pill can make the effect stronger. But I want to be careful here. Placebos mostly affect symptoms that people feel and report, like pain, nausea, or tiredness. A sugar pill won't shrink a tumor or cure an infection.

There's also a flip side, called the nocebo effect. If patients expect side effects, like a headache, some of them will actually get one, even from a pill with nothing in it.

And that's why new drugs are tested against placebos. If patients on the real drug don't do clearly better than patients on the sugar pill, then the drug isn't really working.
